scenes.narration: Your phone knows exactly where you are. Yet it never sends a single signal to ask.
Overhead, about thirty satellites circle the Earth, each one broadcasting the time, over and over.
Your phone listens. It measures how long each signal took to arrive. Light is fast, but not instant, so a longer delay means a farther satellite.
One distance puts you somewhere on a circle. A second narrows it down. A third crosses at a single point. That is where you are.
So GPS is really a stopwatch and some geometry. A fourth satellite even corrects your phone's clock. And your phone only listens. It never sends a thing.

research.notes: MEO ~20,200 km, 2 orbits/day, >=4 satellites visible, ~31 operational (gps.gov). Signal ~67 ms at nadir is own arithmetic (20,200 km / c), not shown on screen. Orbit sizes and ring delays are illustrative, not to scale.
